intro.text: A surgeon in the Alethi town of Hearthstone and the father of Kaladin, whom he trained in medicine from a young age.
An Alethi surgeon of the second nahn from Hearthstone, married to Hesina and the father of Kaladin. He now lives and works in Urithiru, where his home includes a fully equipped surgery.

items.text: As a youth, Lirin travelled to Kharbranth as a courier and met people of many cultures. He had particularly poor luck with Thaylens, every one of whom tried to swindle him.
Back in Alethkar, he trained as a surgeon under Vathe of Shorsebroon, who had himself studied at the Great Concourse of Kharbranth.
Vathe taught him breathing exercises to keep him calm during surgery.

While travelling, Lirin met Hesina, the daughter of a high-ranking family, and they fell in love. His first meeting with her parents was a disaster, but the two married and started a family in Hearthstone.

Lirin trained his son Kaladin as a surgeon from a young age. When Kaladin was ten, they operated together on a girl named Sani and saved four of the five fingers on her injured hand. Afterwards Lirin scolded him for spending time with older boys who idolised soldiers, quizzed him on diseases and remedies, and told him he hoped to send him to study in Kharbranth at sixteen.

Some years on, Kaladin tried and failed to save Miasal, a girl who had fallen from a height. Lirin arrived too late, but after examining her he was impressed by his son's work, and he sat with the weeping Kaladin on the steps of the surgery as the sun set.

Lirin was a close friend of Brightlord Wistiow, Hearthstone's citylord, despite their difference in rank. When Wistiow fell ill in 1165, Lirin could not save him. On the day he died, Lirin drew up a document giving his family a number of diamond broams, and was the only witness to Wistiow approving it. He told Kaladin the spheres would pay for his studies in Kharbranth.

In truth, Wistiow had not been in his right mind in his last days. Lirin and Hesina had arranged the transfer themselves, knowing his death would end any chance of a match between their children. Rumours spread, but nothing was ever proven.

One night, masked townsmen came to rob the family of the spheres. Knowing they were neighbours rather than bandits, Lirin uncovered the spheres and lit up the night, stripping away their anonymity, and the men slunk off.

When the new citylord, Roshone, arrived unannounced, Lirin tried to welcome him, but Roshone sneered and blamed him for Wistiow's death. Lirin likened his arrival to a butcher being played in breakneck: what came next depended on the other player.

Roshone suspected Lirin of stealing the spheres and set out to squeeze them from him. At his urging, the townspeople stopped their donations and raised their prices, though some still left food in secret for Hesina to find.

Once the family's income had dried up, Roshone invited Lirin to dinner, and Kaladin went with him. Lirin refused to eat, haggled over how many spheres he might return, and then left in feigned frustration before any deal was struck.

On the way home, Lirin admitted he had never meant to give up the spheres. He had only wanted to seem to bend, to buy his family a reprieve from a petty man who would not rest until Lirin was broken. Kaladin also learned the truth of how his parents had come by the spheres.

After a disastrous whitespine hunt, Roshone and his son Rillir were brought to Lirin's surgery. Lirin judged Rillir beyond saving and eased his suffering with dazewater, then treated Roshone, despite his screams to save his son. Removing the tusk from Roshone's leg, Lirin could have let him die, but he could not kill someone in his care.

Afterwards, Lirin began spending Wistiow's spheres. The family did not need to, but it let Roshone believe he had won, and Lirin meant to keep up the act until Kaladin turned sixteen and the remaining spheres could go with him to Kharbranth.

In revenge for Rillir, Roshone had Lirin's younger son Tien conscripted; Lirin and Kaladin were exempt as surgeon and assistant. Lirin tried to stop it but was held back by Amaram, who promised to keep Tien out of combat as a messenger. Kaladin enlisted alongside his brother and promised his devastated parents he would bring Tien home.

Tien died within four months of leaving. Kaladin wrote to tell his parents of his failure and that he would not come home; they did not reply. Years afterwards, they received word that Kaladin too had been killed.
A year before the Everstorm, Lirin's third son, Oroden, was born.

After the Everstorm, Kaladin found his father tending the wounded in Roshone's parlour with Hesina and his apprentice Mara. Lirin soon recognised him, and they had a tearful reunion. When Roshone's guards balked at Kaladin's slave brands, Lirin refused to let his son be sent away and offered to buy his writ, then wrote to the highprince's administrators to buy time.

Kaladin slipped back into his old role as assistant while they treated the wounded. Lirin thought war was inevitable but wished his son had no part in it, and he refused Kaladin's offer to move the family to Urithiru, saying Hearthstone needed him.

Under singer occupation, Lirin checked Herdazian refugees for plague on Abiajan's orders, and he and the visiting Kaladin argued often about his role as a Radiant. When a Fused came looking for Kaladin and Kaladin killed a singer in the fight, Lirin was appalled, and he refused to abandon the people of Hearthstone.

So Kaladin evacuated the whole town on the Fourth Bridge. Lirin was curt with Dalinar and grew withdrawn on learning that Radiants could heal, until Kaladin explained its limits; then he grew eager to work in Urithiru's clinic with new equipment from Kharbranth. He was overjoyed to hear Kaladin would leave the army.
When the tower's Radiants fell unconscious, Lirin talked Kaladin out of fighting. But when a Regal came to take the Radiants in his clinic, Kaladin killed him, and Lirin angrily sent his son away.

Lirin and Hesina were put to work caring for the comatose Radiants. He told Venli and Rlain he did not want to fight the occupation, and called the water bearers who wore shash glyphs on their foreheads foolish.
When Dabbid told Lirin and Rlain that Kaladin was dying, Lirin insisted he would heal him but would not promise to keep him from the Fused afterwards.

Hesina told Lirin that Kaladin was the best kind of soldier and introduced him to Noril, who wore the shash glyph because Kaladin had helped him with his depression. She urged Lirin to ask the others why they wore it.

When the tower fell fully to the enemy, Moash handed Lirin to the Pursuer as a hostage. A panicked Heavenly One threw him from the roof, and Kaladin, speaking the Fourth Ideal, caught him. They embraced, and Kaladin said each of their ways was right for them. Lirin, who had put a shash glyph on his own forehead to show faith in his son, found Kaladin's brand finally healed.

Dalinar asked Lirin to help restructure Urithiru's medical system. When Kaladin told his parents he was leaving to track down Ishar, Lirin hugged him in a rare show of affection, and spent the following days treating patients in the tower.

appearance.text: A thin, balding, bespectacled man, several fingers shorter than his wife. He rarely wears his glasses except in surgery, as they would be hard to replace.

personality.text: Lirin predicts highstorms as a hobby and is right about eight times in ten.

Lirin is stubborn and dislikes ambiguity. He avoids needless strife and ignores gossip, but will confront anyone who threatens his family or town. The townsfolk find him strange and uncomfortable to be around, yet respect his work, and he cares about them in turn.

He believes lives are priceless and charges nothing for his work, keeping his surgery meticulously clean. He knows he cannot save everyone, and triages by clear rules: the youngest if wounds are equal, otherwise the worst hurt, but always recognising when a patient is beyond help.
Deeply opposed to violence and to needless danger, Lirin sees no glory in war or the soldier's Calling; he would rather let several people die than kill one himself.
